chunks: "I debug software with the same loop as hardware: reproduce it, observe, split, test one change at a time.
First I get a reliable way to make it fail, ideally a minimal example, and I read what the system is already telling me: compiler warnings, error codes, logs, a stack trace or fault registers.
Then I localize. With a debugger over SWD or JTAG I can set breakpoints, step, and use watchpoints to find who writes a variable.
If it used to work, I use git bisect: a thousand commits is about ten builds. I add assertions to check my assumptions, and unit tests to pin down the behavior.
On an embedded target there are extra tricks.
If I need timing, I toggle a GPIO at the start and end of a function or ISR and watch it on a scope, which measures the real duration without stopping the CPU.
A hard fault gives me the stacked program counter, which tells me where it died.
I check classic causes: stack overflow, uninitialized or out-of-bounds data, non-atomic access to a variable shared with an ISR, a missing volatile, and the watchdog.
And I'm careful about observer effects. A printf at 115200 baud takes milliseconds and can hide a race condition, and a breakpoint stops the timers.
When a bug vanishes under the debugger, that itself is a clue. After the fix, I add a test so it can't come back."
